scams.name: Fake Parking Ticket QR Code
scams.tldr: Scammers in Georgetown and National Mall parking areas place fake DC parking citations with QR codes on windshields of out-of-state vehicles, directing victims to fraudulent payment sites that charge $75–$150 and capture credit-card data for additional unauthorized purchases.
scams.description:
You return to your rental car parked in Georgetown or near the National Mall and find what looks like an official DC parking citation tucked under the windshield wiper. The ticket is convincingly printed with city government logos, a department name, and a violation code. If you are from out of state you have no basis for comparison, and the format looks authoritative enough that most tourists assume it is real.

The ticket includes a QR code labeled "Pay Online." Scanning it opens a site that mimics the official DC payment portal — the URL ends in .com rather than .gov, but the design is close enough that most people do not check. You enter your credit card number and pay the $75–$150 fine. The payment reaches scammers, not the city, and your card details are then used for additional unauthorized charges. The DC DMV confirmed it does not issue parking tickets at all; all legitimate DC citations come from the DC Department of Transportation or Metropolitan Police and are only payable through .gov websites.

Never scan a QR code on a parking ticket — go directly to dmv.dc.gov and look up your plate number to check whether any real violation exists . A legitimate DC citation directs you only to .gov payment portals and lists the Metropolitan Police or DC Department of Transportation as the issuing authority; any ticket naming the DC DMV as the issuer or pointing to a .com URL is fake. Photograph suspicious tickets and report them to the DC DMV at (202) 737-4404.
scams.avoidance: Only pay DC parking tickets through the official DC DMV website at dmv.dc.gov or by mail to the address listed on legitimate tickets. Check the issuing agency: legitimate DC tickets come from the DC Department of Transportation (DDOT) or Metropolitan Police, never from 'DC DMV.' Never scan a QR code on a parking ticket; instead, go directly to the official website and search for your violation by plate number. Take a photo of the ticket and compare it with official DC citation examples available on the DC government website. Report suspicious tickets to the DC DMV at (202) 737-4404 and file a complaint with the Better Business Bureau.
scams.location: Georgetown streets, National Mall parking areas, Dupont Circle metered spots, any street with out-of-state plates

scams.name: Metro Station Change Scam
scams.tldr: A scammer in a busy DC Metro station holds up two $10 bills and asks a tourist to exchange them for a $20, then palms the $20 and claims the tourist only handed over $1 — victims lose $19–$45 in a transaction that plays out in under thirty seconds.
scams.description:
You are moving through the Smithsonian or Gallery Place Metro station, maybe consulting your phone for the next transfer, when someone approaches holding up two $10 bills. "Can you break these for a twenty?" The request seems routine and harmless — a few seconds of helpfulness. The Smithsonian station is a particular hotspot because of the constant tourist flow heading to the National Mall.

You hand over a $20 bill. The scammer briefly shuffles both hands, then shows you a $1 bill — insisting that is what you gave them. In the busy, rushed station environment the swap happened in a blink and you are uncertain what you saw. A variant involves asking to break a $50 bill, then returning $5 bills folded to look like $20s. The scammer often works with a partner who creates a secondary distraction if the first exchange attempt is questioned.

Say "no" and keep walking without engaging — never make change for a stranger in a Metro station under any circumstances . The specific setup of two small bills for one large one has no legitimate use case: anyone genuinely needing change uses a vending machine. If someone persists, walk toward the station manager booth; the scam collapses in front of a Metro employee.
scams.avoidance: Never make change for strangers in Metro stations or on the street; politely say 'no' and keep walking. If someone needs Metro fare help, direct them to the station manager booth rather than giving cash. Keep large bills in a secure wallet and avoid displaying cash in crowded transit areas. Be especially alert at Smithsonian, Gallery Place, and Union Station Metro stops, which are prime hunting grounds. If you feel pressured, walk toward the station manager booth or a Metro Transit Police officer.
scams.location: Smithsonian Metro station, Gallery Place-Chinatown Metro, Union Station entrance, L'Enfant Plaza Metro concourse

scams.name: Unlicensed Pedicab Price Gouging
scams.tldr: Unlicensed pedicab operators on the National Mall quote no fare before boarding, then demand $50–$120 for a 10-minute ride once the trip is over — on National Park Service property where most commercial pedicab pickups are not authorized.
scams.description:
You are walking the National Mall on a warm afternoon between the Washington Monument and the Lincoln Memorial when a pedicab driver pulls alongside. The distance feels long and your feet are tired. The driver is friendly, mentions the monuments ahead, and says nothing about price when you ask — "we'll work it out." You board, the ride is comfortable, and you arrive.

The driver produces a per-minute rate of $5–$8 that was never mentioned before boarding, or announces a flat "private tour" charge of $80–$120. You are now standing on the Mall with no receipt, no prior agreement, and a driver who will not leave until you pay. The National Park Service holds exclusive commercial transportation rights on the Mall through Tourmobile; most pedicabs picking up passengers there are operating illegally and have no accountability if the price is disputed. Cherry blossom season intensifies the problem as dense crowds make walking harder and unlicensed drivers aggressively solicit overwhelmed tourists.

Confirm the total fare in dollars before you sit down and refuse to board any driver who will not give a written or displayed price upfront — licensed operators like Nonpartisan Pedicab post rates of $84–$90 per hour clearly before you board. The free DC Circulator bus ($1 per ride) and National Park Service shuttles are also legitimate alternatives to walking the 2-mile length of the Mall.
scams.avoidance: Only use pedicab services that display clear per-hour pricing and are licensed by the National Park Service, such as Nonpartisan Pedicab. Always confirm the total fare, whether it is per trip or per hour, and get a verbal agreement before boarding. Take a photo of the rate card and the pedicab's license number before the ride begins. Walk the National Mall instead; the distance from the Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial is about 2 miles and manageable for most visitors. Use the free National Mall shuttle or DC Circulator bus ($1) as cheaper legitimate alternatives.
scams.location: National Mall between the Capitol and Lincoln Memorial, around the Washington Monument, Jefferson Memorial area, Tidal Basin during cherry blossom season

scams.name: Friendship Bracelet and CD Hustle
scams.tldr: Street performers near the National Mall and outside Smithsonian museums tie bracelets onto tourists' wrists or press CDs into their hands before demanding $10–$20 as a "donation" — a second person often uses the distraction to pickpocket a nearby bag or pocket.
scams.description:
You are walking near the Washington Monument or outside a Smithsonian museum entrance when someone approaches with a wide smile and a colorful bracelet or a plastic-sleeve CD. "This is free — just want you to hear my music," or "A friendship bracelet, for good luck." The gesture feels friendly and the item looks inexpensive. Before you can respond, the bracelet is already being tied around your wrist or the CD is in your hand.

Once you have the item, the tone shifts. The "donation" is $10–$20 and is not optional. Returning the bracelet or CD is resisted — "it's already on you" or "I already gave it to you." If you try to walk away, the person becomes loud and follows. While this exchange holds your attention, a second person nearby may be unzipping your bag or reaching into a side pocket — the confrontation is the distraction.

Keep your hands in your pockets and say a firm "no" without slowing down — once you accept the item, the payment demand follows immediately . If a bracelet is tied on before you can pull back, remove it and place it on the ground without argument; you are not legally obligated to pay for an unsolicited item. Keep your bag zipped across your front during any unexpected street interaction near the Mall or Smithsonian entrances.
scams.avoidance: Keep your hands in your pockets or at your sides and firmly say 'No thank you' without breaking stride. Never allow a stranger to place anything on your body; physically step back if someone reaches for your wrist. If a bracelet is tied on, remove it and place it on the ground; you are not obligated to pay for unsolicited items. Keep your bag zipped and in front of you during any street interaction, especially near the National Mall. If someone becomes aggressive, walk toward the nearest Park Police officer or into a Smithsonian museum entrance.
scams.location: National Mall near the Washington Monument, outside Smithsonian museums, Georgetown M Street, Adams Morgan on weekend nights

scams.name: Three-Card Monte Gambling Hustle
scams.tldr: A Three-Card Monte dealer near Union Station and Gallery Place runs a rigged card game with 4–6 planted shills posing as winning spectators — tourists who bet after watching others "win" lose $50–$300 through sleight of hand they cannot detect or overcome.
scams.description:
A small crowd has gathered around a person shuffling three cards on a cardboard box near Union Station or along a busy sidewalk off Pennsylvania Avenue. Several spectators are watching closely; one of them exclaims at a near-miss, another wins and pockets a bill. The game looks fast but beatable if you pay close attention. The dealer smiles and invites you to try.

Your first small bet of $10 or $20 wins. "You've got a good eye." You bet $50 or $100 on the next round and lose. The Metropolitan Police Department states plainly: the only time you win is when the dealer lets you, and the only reason the dealer lets you is to make you believe you can beat them. The winning spectators are paid shills. A card-fold technique ensures the winning card is never where it appears to be regardless of how carefully you tracked it. Lookouts at the corner watch for police; the operation packs up and moves within seconds if needed.

Walk past without stopping to watch — even as a spectator you can be targeted by pickpockets working the edge of the crowd . The people winning at the table are accomplices, not lucky strangers; no attention level or pattern recognition overcomes the dealer's sleight of hand. Three-Card Monte is illegal street gambling in DC; report operations to the Metropolitan Police at (202) 727-9099.
scams.avoidance: Never participate in street gambling games; the game is mathematically rigged through sleight of hand and you cannot win. Walk past without stopping to watch, as even spectators can be targeted by pickpockets working with the group. Understand that the people 'winning' are planted accomplices, not random lucky tourists. Report Three-Card Monte operations to the Metropolitan Police at (202) 727-9099 or 911. Remember that street gambling is illegal in DC and participants can be cited as well as victims.
scams.location: Near Union Station, Gallery Place-Chinatown sidewalks, busy intersections along Pennsylvania Avenue, downtown street corners

scams.name: Fake Tour Guide Solicitation
scams.tldr: Self-appointed "guides" outside the White House, Capitol steps, and Lincoln Memorial approach tourists offering personalized tours for $20–$50 per person, collect cash upfront, then deliver 15 minutes of basic facts before disappearing — all for information the National Park Service provides for free.
scams.description:
You are standing outside the White House fence on Pennsylvania Avenue or near the Capitol steps when someone in a professional-looking jacket approaches: "I can give you a private tour — I know all the history, inside stories, very good." Their opening sentences are fluent and their price of $25–$50 per person sounds reasonable for a guided experience at a major landmark. They ask for cash before starting.

The tour delivers 15–20 minutes of information freely available on the official NPS site, mixed with fabricated historical anecdotes. Some guides steer groups into specific souvenir shops where they receive commissions, spending more time there than at actual sites. Others abruptly end the tour citing a "schedule conflict" and walk away. A common variant involves claiming to have "reserved spots" at the Capitol, Bureau of Engraving, or Smithsonian museums — all of which are free through official channels and require no third-party assistance.

Book tours only through verified companies with TripAdvisor or GetYourGuide profiles before you arrive — a confirmed booking makes street solicitation irrelevant . Every National Mall memorial has free National Park Service ranger-led talks throughout the day; the Capitol, White House, and Bureau of Engraving offer free official tours bookable through .gov reservation systems. Never pay anyone who approaches you unsolicited outside a monument or museum.
scams.avoidance: Book tours only through established companies with verifiable websites, TripAdvisor profiles, and posted reviews. Take advantage of free National Park Service ranger-led walks and talks at all Mall memorials and monuments. Reserve free Capitol, White House, and Bureau of Engraving tours through official.gov websites well in advance. All Smithsonian museums are free; never pay anyone for 'skip the line' access to these institutions. If you want a paid tour, book through platforms like Viator or GetYourGuide where reviews and refund policies are transparent.
scams.location: Outside the White House on Pennsylvania Avenue, near the Capitol steps, around the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, Arlington Cemetery entrance

scams.name: Distraction Pickpocketing on the Metro
scams.tldr: Teams of two or three pickpockets on crowded DC Metro trains and escalators use deliberate bumps, dropped items, or direction questions to distract tourists while a partner lifts wallets, phones, or passports — victims typically lose $300–$1,200 and do not notice until they try to pay for something later.
scams.description:
You board a Metro train at Gallery Place or Metro Center heading toward the National Mall during the morning rush or after a Smithsonian visit. The car is crowded, bags press against other passengers, and everyone is focused on their phone or the route map. The Smithsonian station escalators during peak season and Gallery Place during sports events create particularly tight conditions. Nothing looks unusual.

One person bumps into you harder than the crowd justifies, or someone near your feet dramatically drops something and makes you look down, or a person beside you asks an overly detailed question about which line to take while standing unusually close. These three or four seconds of redirected attention are the window: a second person behind or beside you has opened your bag zipper, slipped into your back pocket, or pulled your phone from a loosely held hand. Losses range from wallet contents to a $300–$1,200 phone plus the downstream damage from stolen card numbers and identity data.

Carry your wallet in a front pocket and keep your bag zipped and positioned in front of your body on Metro platforms and trains — a bag on your back in a crowded DC Metro car is an accessible target. Stay especially alert on escalators at Smithsonian, Metro Center, and Gallery Place stations, and avoid using your phone while walking through crowded station corridors. Report pickpocketing to Metro Transit Police at (202) 962-2121 and cancel stolen cards immediately.
scams.avoidance: Carry your wallet in a front pocket and keep your bag zipped and positioned in front of your body at all times on the Metro. Use a money belt or neck wallet for your passport, large cash, and backup credit card when touring the city. Be especially vigilant on escalators at Smithsonian, Metro Center, and Gallery Place stations during peak tourist season. Keep your phone secured and avoid using it while walking through crowded station corridors. Report pickpocketing immediately to Metro Transit Police at (202) 962-2121 and cancel stolen cards right away.
scams.location: Gallery Place-Chinatown station, Metro Center transfer platform, crowded Orange/Blue/Silver line trains, Smithsonian station escalators
